title: Almost all pure entangled states enable unbounded nonlocality sharing
authors: Anna Steffinlongo, Nicola D'Alessandro, Martin J. Renner
abstract: We establish a connection between Hardy's paradox and nonlocality sharing in sequential bipartite scenarios, where each subsystem is measured in turn by a chain of observers. We show that any correlations exhibiting a Hardy paradox in the two-input two-output scenario enable sequential violations of the CHSH inequality between arbitrarily many pairs of observers, using only projective measurements and the assistance of a small local ancilla system. Since almost all pure entangled states, with the only exception of the maximally entangled one, admit Hardy correlations, our protocol applies generically: almost all pure entangled states, if assisted by a local ancilla, allow for nonlocality sharing between arbitrarily many observer pairs using only projective measurements.
summary: The paper proves that almost all pure entangled states possess the capability to share nonlocality among an arbitrary number of observers. This is achieved by linking the phenomenon to Hardy's paradox and constructing a protocol using local ancillas and projective measurements. It establishes that two-sided nonlocality sharing is a generic feature of quantum entanglement.
main_problem: The paper establishes a general connection between Hardy's paradox correlations and the ability to share nonlocality among an arbitrarily large number of distant observer pairs in sequential bipartite measurements.
main_result: It is shown that almost all pure entangled quantum states (excluding the maximally entangled state) can facilitate two-sided nonlocality sharing using only projective measurements and a small local ancilla system.
method: The authors use the CHSH inequality as a diagnostic tool, linking its violation to the existence of Hardy correlations within the shared entangled state in a sequential measurement protocol.
model_or_system: The model involves a bipartite quantum system ($	ext{|\Psiangle_{AB}}$) distributed to two parties (Alice and Bob), who then perform sequential measurements assisted by local ancilla qubits or qutrits.
key_observables: CHSH value ($S$), which must exceed the classical bound of $3/4$; Hardy correlations, characterized by specific zero probabilities in correlation tables.
important_parameters: The entanglement structure of the state (Schmidt coefficients $\lambda_i$); measurement strategies defined by parameters like $\alpha,  eta, \gamma$.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the availability of a local memory register/ancilla to track measurement history and that measurements are projective.

paper_structure: The paper builds by first connecting Hardy's paradox to nonlocality sharing in a general bipartite setting. It then develops a protocol using an ancilla to demonstrate simultaneous CHSH violation across multiple pairs of observers, culminating in the proof that this is generic for most entangled states.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful demonstration of how fundamental quantum correlations (Hardy paradox) can be leveraged to establish robust, scalable nonlocality resources necessary for quantum communication protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Sequential scenario considered in this work. A source distributes a pure entangled state together with two quantum ancillas ρ = ρAB ⊗ρA′ ⊗ρB′ = |Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|AB ⊗|no⟩⟨no|A′ ⊗|no⟩⟨no|B′ to chains of observers on Alice’s and Bob’s sides. For convenience, the ancillas are included in the initial state distributed by the source, so that all observers perform the same operation. Equivalently, they could be prepared locally by the first observers. Each observer may perform a projective measurement or pass the system to the next observer.
